Here are the verse-by-verse notes compiled from the available sources, following the rules for citation.

---

## 2 Samuel 5 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 – "Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, 'Here we are, your own flesh and blood.'"

**Traditional Reading:** After the death of Ish-bosheth (2 Samuel 4), the northern tribes, who had previously followed Saul's house, finally turn to David. The phrase "your bone and your flesh" is a Hebrew idiom meaning blood relatives (cf. Gen 29:14; Judg 9:2). The tribes acknowledge their common descent from Jacob/Israel, and David's godly response to the unjust deaths of Abner and Ish-bosheth contributed to their willingness to seek him as king. 1 Chronicles 12:23–40 describes a great assembly of over 340,000 warriors who gathered at Hebron with "a loyal heart" and "one mind" to make David king.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-5/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-5-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-5.html (Ellicott)

**Methodist (Clarke):** Clarke notes that after Ish-bosheth and Abner were dead, the tribes "had no hope of maintaining a separate kingdom, and therefore thought it better to submit to David's authority." He lists three good arguments the tribes made: David was their countryman, had proven his military leadership, and had a divine appointment.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-samuel-5.html

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** Guzik observes, "It's sad that the tribes only turned to David when their previous choice was taken away. On the same principle, it's sad when Christians only finally recognize Jesus as King when their other choices fail."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-5/

---

### v. 2 – "Even in times past, while Saul was king over us, you were the one who led Israel out and brought them back. And to you the LORD said, 'You will shepherd My people Israel, and you will be ruler over them.'"

**Traditional Reading:** Three reasons are given why David should be king: (1) kinship ("your bone and flesh," v.1), (2) proven military leadership ("led out and brought in" — the language of a successful commander who leads troops to battle and back in victory, cf. 1 Sam 18:13,16), and (3) divine election — the LORD had promised David he would "shepherd" (Hebrew *ra'ah*) His people. The shepherd imagery is powerful: it echoes God as Shepherd (Ps 23), Moses as shepherd (Num 27:17), and points forward to the Messiah (Jn 10:11). The exact words of the divine promise are not quoted verbatim elsewhere but may summarise Samuel's words at David's anointing or Abner's earlier statement (2 Sam 3:18).

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-5-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-5.html (Ellicott)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-5/

**Methodist (Clarke):** Clarke emphasises that in ancient times Greek kings were called *poimenes laou* ("shepherds of the people"), noting that all good kings were truly such. He contrasts the British constitution, under which the king is a "patriotic king" and "father of his people," with despotic governments.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-samuel-5.html

**Precept Austin (Butler):** John Butler notes that David's responsibilities ("feed my people") are stressed before his rank ("captain over Israel"): "Most men are interested in the 'captain' privilege but not very interested in their feeding responsibilities."

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-5-commentary

---

### v. 3 – "So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, where King David made with them a covenant before the LORD. And they anointed him king over Israel."

**Traditional Reading:** This is David's **third anointing**: (1) privately by Samuel in Bethlehem (1 Sam 16:13), (2) by the men of Judah over the house of Judah (2 Sam 2:4), and now (3) by all Israel over the united kingdom. Adam Clarke distinguishes: "By his anointing by Samuel he acquired *jus ad regnum*, a right to the kingdom; and by his present anointing he had a *jus in regno*, authority over the kingdom." The Hebrew verb for "made a covenant" is *karath* ("cut"), suggesting an animal sacrifice sealing the agreement. The covenant was "before the LORD," meaning Yahweh witnessed and sanctioned it. Some (Ellicott) suggest the "league" addressed specific matters such as military leadership, treatment of Saul's remaining house, and impartiality between tribes.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-5-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-samuel-5.html (Clarke)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-5.html (Ellicott)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** Guzik highlights the three characteristics of godly leadership evident here: belonging to God's people in heritage and heart, demonstrated capability to lead, and an evident call from God.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-5/

**Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics):** Notes that the covenant involved obligations on both sides — David pledged to rule according to God's will (Deut 17:16–20), and the people pledged obedience according to the same will. "The Law of God was the rule and square of his government, whereunto both prince and people are sworn."

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/2_samuel/5.htm

---

### vv. 4–5 – "David was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned forty years. In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah."

**Traditional Reading:** David was anointed by Samuel at about age 15, meaning he spent roughly **15 years in preparation** before taking the throne at 30 — a detail many commentators see as teaching that "great tasks require great preparation." The 40-year reign (7½ in Hebron, 33 in Jerusalem) makes David 70 at his death (Ellicott). The six months are usually omitted in summary statements (as in v. 4 and 1 Chr 29:27), with the sacred historians either rounding down or counting fractional years as whole ones.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-5/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-5.html (Ellicott)
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-5-commentary

**Precept Austin:** "David has been in God's school of training men for kingship for some 10 years, most of this time as a fugitive and under difficult circumstances."

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-5-commentary

**Denominational note:** No significant denominational differences were found on these verses; all traditions read them as straightforward historical summary.

---

### vv. 6–7 – "Now the king and his men marched to Jerusalem against the Jebusites… David captured the fortress of Zion (that is, the City of David)."

**Traditional Reading:** Jerusalem (also called Jebus, 1 Chr 11:4) was still a Canaanite enclave in the centre of Israel, roughly 400 years after the Conquest. Its location on a ridge surrounded by deep valleys on three sides made it easily defensible. David attacked it immediately after his coronation, recognising its strategic value: it had no prior tribal association (good for a unified kingdom), was centrally located, and was naturally defensible. Ellicott notes that the king of Jerusalem had been slain by Joshua (Josh 10:23–26), and Judah had taken and burned the city (Judg 1:7–8), but it was only partially occupied by Israelites and later fell back entirely into Jebusite hands (Judg 19:11–12).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-5.html (Ellicott)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-5/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-samuel-5.html (Clarke)

**Methodist (Clarke):** Clarke says the Jebusites "vainly confiding in the strength of their fortress" taunted David, and that David "very properly began his reign over the whole country by the siege of this city."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-samuel-5.html

---

### v. 8 – "On that day he said, 'Whoever attacks the Jebusites must use the water shaft to reach the lame and blind who are despised by David.' That is why it is said, 'The blind and the lame will never enter the palace.'"

**Traditional Reading:** This is one of the most difficult verses in the chapter. The Hebrew word *tsinnor* ("water shaft" / "gutter" / "waterspout") occurs only here and in Ps 42:7. Several interpretations exist:

(1) The **water shaft theory:** David's men climbed up through the city's water tunnel. This is often connected with "Warren's Shaft," discovered by Charles Warren in 1867, which connected the Gihon Spring to the stronghold on the southeastern hill. Joab led the assault and was rewarded with command of the army (1 Chr 11:6).

(2) **Ellicott's reading:** "Whosoever smites the Jebusites, let him hurl into the watercourses (i.e., down the precipice) the lame and the blind." David turns the Jebusites' own taunt back on them — calling all Jebusite defenders "the lame and blind" and ordering them thrown down the precipice without quarter, since the Canaanites were under the old ban.

(3) The **proverb** ("the blind and the lame will never enter the palace") arose from this event, used of any hated or unwelcome persons.

The 1 Chronicles 11:6 parallel adds: "David said, 'Whoever smites the Jebusites first shall be chief and captain.' So Joab the son of Zeruiah went up first and was chief." This explains why Joab became commander of all Israel's armies (not just Judah's) and sheds light on David's later sense of obligation toward him (Ellicott).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-5.html (Ellicott)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/5-9.html (StudyLight on v.9, discussing the shaft)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/2-samuel-5.html (Barnes)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-5/

**Methodist (Clarke):** Clarke, quoting Kennicott, reconstructs the text: "Thou shalt not come in hither; for the blind and the lame shall drive thee away by saying, 'David shall not come in hither.'" He thinks the Jebusites placed literal blind and lame people on the walls to mock David's assault.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-samuel-5.html

---

### v. 9 – "So David took up residence in the fortress and called it the City of David. He built it up all the way around, from the supporting terraces inward."

**Traditional Reading:** "The stronghold" (same word as v.7) became David's residence. He renamed it "the City of David." "Millo" (translated "supporting terraces" in BSB) is a Hebrew word meaning "filling." It was probably an old Canaanite fortification or earthwork on the northern end of Mount Zion, since on all other sides Zion was protected by precipitous ravines (Ellicott). Subsequent kings — Solomon (1 Kgs 11:27) and Hezekiah (2 Chr 32:5) — added to its strength.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-5.html (Ellicott)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/2-samuel-5.html (Barnes)

---

### vv. 10–12 – "And David became greater and greater, for the LORD God of Hosts was with him. Now Hiram king of Tyre sent envoys… And David realized that the LORD had established him as king…"

**Traditional Reading:** David's greatness came from God's presence, not merely military skill. Hiram of Tyre (the same Hiram who later befriended Solomon) sent cedar, carpenters, and stonemasons to build David a palace — indicating that David had become a recognised international figure who could form political alliances, not merely a warrior. Ellicott notes that this embassy may have occurred years after the conquest of Jerusalem, as David "went on and grew great." The Israelites had little skill in architecture and relied on Phoenician craftsmen.

David perceived three things (Guzik): (1) the LORD had established him, (2) the kingdom belonged to God, and (3) his exaltation was "for the sake of His people Israel" — not for David's personal aggrandisement. The Pulpit Homiletics adds: "David's prosperity had not blinded him to the fact that his blessings came to him as the head of the theocracy."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-5/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-5.html (Ellicott)
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/2_samuel/5.htm (Pulpit Homiletics)

---

### vv. 13–16 – "After he had arrived from Hebron, David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem…"

**Traditional Reading:** This was in direct disobedience to Deuteronomy 17:17: "Neither shall he multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away." Commentators across traditions agree this was a moral failure. David already had several wives (Ahinoam, Abigail, Maacah, Haggith, Abital, Eglah, and Michal — though Michal was taken from him). Eleven sons are named here (with variations in spelling compared to 1 Chr 3:5–8 and 14:4–7). The first four — Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon — were born to Bathsheba (1 Chr 3:5), placing their births later in David's reign, though listed here for convenience. Solomon is placed last yet was likely the oldest of Bathsheba's sons (2 Sam 12:24).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-5/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-5.html (Ellicott)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** "It is often true that the seeds to our future trouble are sown in times of great success and prosperity. In some ways, David handled trials better than success." Most of David's later troubles — the Bathsheba affair, Amnon and Tamar, Absalom's rebellion — stemmed from relationships with women and children.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-5/

**Methodist (Clarke):** Clarke calculates David had eight wives and ten concubines before this addition, and remarks: "That dispensation permitted polygamy, but from the beginning it was not so; and as upon an average there are about fourteen males born to thirteen females, polygamy is unnatural."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-samuel-5.html

**Denominational note:** All Protestant traditions agree that David's polygamy was a deviation from God's original design (Gen 2:24) and a violation of the specific command for kings in Deut 17:17. None defend it. The difference is one of emphasis: Reformed/Calvinist commentators may stress God's sovereign grace in using a flawed king; Wesleyan/Holiness commentators may stress the warning against disobedience in times of success.

---

### vv. 17–19 – Philistine invasion; David inquires of the LORD

**Traditional Reading:** Upon hearing that David was now king over united Israel, the Philistines mobilised to crush him before his power consolidated. The Philistines had occupied much of Israel since Saul's death (Clarke). David "went down to the stronghold" — not the citadel of Zion, but some defensive position near the Philistine encampment (Ellicott), perhaps the cave of Adullam or a similar refuge. The Valley of Rephaim ("valley of the giants," Josh 15:8) was a fertile valley stretching about three miles south and southwest from Jerusalem. Critically, David "inquired of the LORD" before acting — a pattern of dependence on God that marks his successes.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-5.html (Ellicott)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-samuel-5.html (Clarke)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-5/

---

### vv. 20–21 – "Baal-perazim… the Philistines abandoned their idols"

**Traditional Reading:** David attacked with overwhelming force — "like a bursting flood." The name *Baal-perazim* means "Lord (or possessor) of breaches," commemorating how the LORD broke through the enemy lines. Ellicott clarifies the name has no connection to the Canaanite deity Baal but means "possessor of breaches." The Philistines carried their idols into battle (as Israel once carried the ark, 1 Sam 4), and in their panic abandoned them on the field. 1 Chronicles 14:12 adds that David burned them, in obedience to Deuteronomy 7:5.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-5.html (Ellicott)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-samuel-5.html (Clarke)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-5/

---

### vv. 22–25 – Second battle in the Valley of Rephaim; the sound in the balsam trees

**Traditional Reading:** This is the most theologically rich section. The Philistines regrouped in the same valley. Rather than assuming the same strategy would work again, David inquired of the LORD again. God gave a **different** directive: circle around behind them and wait by the balsam (or mulberry) trees. When David heard "the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees," he was to "advance quickly" (KJV: "bestir thyself"), for that sound signalled that the LORD had gone out before him to strike the enemy camp.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-5/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-5.html (Ellicott)
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-5-commentary

**Pentecostal/Charismatic emphasis (Guzik/Spurgeon):** Guzik, quoting Spurgeon, says of the rustling sound: "As the Rabbis have it, and it is a very pretty conceit if it be true, the footsteps of angels walking along the tops of the mulberry trees make them rustle." The spiritual application is that when believers sense God at work, they must "advance quickly" and join Him in victory, rather than stirring up others — they must "bestir thyself." Guzik adds that Spurgeon applied this to prayer and devotion: "When we see the work of God happening around us, it is like the sound in the mulberry trees — the rustling sound should awaken us to prayer and devotion."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-5/

**Methodist (Clarke):** Clarke suggests the supernatural sign was necessary so "David might have thought that the sleight or *ruse de guerre* which he had used was the cause of his victory." God confirmed His direct involvement. Clarke then asks a searching question: "How is it that such supernatural directions and assistances are not communicated now? Because they are not asked for; and they are not asked for because they are not expected; and they are not expected because men have not faith; and they have not faith because they are under a refined spirit of atheism, and have no spiritual intercourse with their Maker."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-samuel-5.html

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** The Baptist commentary emphasises David's dependence on God's will before acting — "David did not act without knowing the will of the Lord" — and notes that the decisive victory renamed the battlefield.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/2-samuel-5.html

**Anglican (Ellicott):** The word translated "marching" is the same used of "the march of the hosts of the Lord" in Judges 5:4 and Psalm 68:7 — suggesting a theophanic military procession. The pursuit stretched from Gibeon (about 5½ miles NW of Jerusalem) to Gezer on the edge of the Philistine plain — some 18 miles total.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-5.html (Ellicott)

---

### Summary of Denominational Distinctives Observed

| Issue | Distinctive |
|---|---|
| **David's polygamy (vv.13–16)** | All traditions condemn it as disobedience to Deut 17:17. Pentecostals (Guzik) stress it as "seeds of future trouble sown in success." Methodists (Clarke) add a natural-law argument against polygamy. Reformed sources would likely stress God's sovereign grace despite David's failure (though not directly found in searched pages for this chapter). |
| **The "sound in the trees" (v.24)** | Pentecostal/Charismatic: stresses supernatural angelic activity (Spurgeon/Guzik). Methodist (Clarke): stresses that God provides supernatural signs because we would otherwise credit human strategy. Baptist: emphasises simple obedience to God's direction. Anglican (Ellicott): ties the "marching" language to OT theophany traditions (Judg 5:4; Ps 68:7). |
| **The covenant (v.3)** | All traditions see this as a mutual, binding agreement. The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics) stresses its "theocratic" character — limiting the king's power under God's law. Reformed covenant theology would see this as an outworking of God's sovereign covenant with David. |
| **David's anointing (v.3)** | No significant difference: all traditions note the three anointings and their progressive nature — private, tribal, national. Methodists (Clarke) add the *jus ad regnum* / *jus in regno* distinction. |

### Views Not Found

- **Catholic / Orthodox readings:** Searches of newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org returned no verse-by-verse material on 2 Samuel 5 within the search limits.
- **Modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org):** Not reached due to search/fetch limits.
- **Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org):** No distinct Lutheran material on this chapter was found within limits.
- **Reformed (ligonier.org, monergism.com):** No chapter-specific material from these sites was found within limits, though Reformed principles (divine sovereignty, covenant) are implicit in the traditional readings above.
- **Prosperity / Word of Faith / Hyper-grace:** No material from these traditions was found for this chapter.
